newsitem.title: UK: BoE moves seen strengthening anti-inflation stance.
newsitem.headline: BoE moves seen strengthening anti-inflation stance.

text.p: British financial experts believed Thursday's appointment of two new deputy governors reinforces the anti-inflation credentials of the Bank of England's interest rate setting monetary policy committee.

Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair's office confirmed the appointment of top investment banker David Clementi, an ex-vice chairman at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson, to replace outgoing deputy governor Howard Davies.

But in a surprise move which pleased financial markets, it added that arch-inflation hawk Mervyn King -- the central bank's chief economist -- would take up the new position of second deputy governor in charge of monetary policy, which is due to be created in the autumn.

The overall composition of the monetary policy committee reflects the government's desire to show that it is pro-business, determined to ensure that Britain escapes from the cycle of boom and bust that has plagued it for decades, economists said.
Clementi's appointment was widely expected after a series of newspaper leaks, but there had been talk that Goldman Sachs chief economist Gavyn Davies would get the second position.

"People were worried that if Mervyn was passed over he might leave," one economist and ex-Bank of England official said. "He's built himself a good reputation for being tough on inflation and the markets trust him."

King's importance to the markets had increased markedly since the Bank of England began publishing quarterly assessments of the British inflation environment in February 1993 and holding on-the-record briefings on its view of the economy, replacing the old unattributable sessions.

"There's nothing in the report itself," said another economist who did not want to be named. "The language tiptoes around. It's only from what King says in the briefing that we know what the Bank really thinks."

King's role has become even more important since May 6, when Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown empowered the central bank to set interest rates to hit the official inflation target of 2.5 percent.
"Mervyn is definitely seen as the best man for the job. Bringing someone else in might have meant diluting the committee in terms of attitude to inflation," another ex-bank official said.
There was less comment on the appointment of Clementi for the simple reason that nothing is known of his attitude to the economy.

At the moment, financial market operators are taking his leading role in the former Conservative administration's 1980s privatisation programme as a sign that he is likely to be another inflation hawk on the MPC.

If that were so, he would line up alongside King, Bank of England Governor Eddie George, Executive Director Ian Plenderleith, London School of Economics (LSE) Professor Charles Goodhart and Sir Alan Budd, once Budd has retired as chief economic adviser at the Treasury.

Economists said King's appointment effectively ruled out a role at the central bank for Gavyn Davies, who had been widely touted for one of the deputy governor positions or even to take over as governor when George's first term expires next year.

"Gavyn Davies and Mervyn would not be a dream team. I think Eddie will be reappointed next year and that can only be a good thing. It might damage the government's credibility if they replaced a central banker with a proven track record with someone who is seen as having close links with Labour," said another ex-bank official.
King is already on the MPC in his capacity as executive director at the central bank so his promotion leaves a vacancy on the committee.

Ex-Bank of England employees say there is no obvious candidate within the ranks of the central bank and LSE professor Charlie Bean may be a strong candidate for King's job. "Bean is a very, very bright man. I'd put my money on him," said another former Bank official.

There is speculation that the role of the Treasury's new Council of Economic Advisers, yet to be appointed, could be beefed up and that Gavyn Davies could be put in charge of it. The next meeting of the monetary policy committee is on August 6 and 7 and analysts say there is a chance of a fourth increase in British interest rates in as many months. Another 1/4 point rise would take official rates to 7.0 percent.
Clementi will not take up his position until September, when another outsider, DeAnne Julius of British Airways, will also join.
Voting members at next week's meeting will be George, King, Plenderleith, Goodhart and Cambridge economist Willem Buiter.
